title: Functional Mushrooms and Alcohol: Lion's Mane, Reishi, Chaga
excerpt: Can you drink on lion's mane, reishi, chaga, or cordyceps? What the research says about functional mushrooms and alcohol, the real risks, timing, and hangover claims.
metaDescription: Can you drink on lion's mane, reishi, or chaga? How functional mushrooms interact with alcohol, the real risks, timing, and whether they help hangovers.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** for most healthy adults, taking a normal dose of lion's mane, reishi, chaga, cordyceps, or turkey tail and having a few drinks is not a known dangerous combination. There are no reports of serious reactions from that pairing alone. But there are also almost no human studies that tested any of these mushrooms with alcohol, so "no known problem" mostly means "nobody has looked closely." The real risks are indirect: reishi can add to alcohol's drowsiness and may thin the blood slightly, chaga is very high in oxalate and has been linked to kidney damage in heavy users, several mushrooms can lower blood sugar, and rare liver injury has been reported with reishi powder. And there is no good evidence that any functional mushroom prevents or treats a hangover.

**The quick rules:** Keep drinking light on days you take these supplements. Take reishi in the morning rather than at bedtime on nights you drink. Don't use chaga daily in large amounts, especially if you drink regularly or have kidney problems. If you take blood thinners, diabetes medication, blood pressure medication, sedatives, or immune-suppressing drugs, talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining any of these with alcohol. And don't count on a mushroom blend to undo a heavy night.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article summarizes general research and is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before combining functional mushrooms and alcohol if** you take blood thinners, diabetes or blood pressure medication, sedatives or sleep aids, or drugs that suppress the immune system; if you have liver or kidney disease; or if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or have surgery coming up. **Stop the supplement and get checked if** you notice yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pain under your right ribs, unusual bruising or bleeding, a rash or swelling, or trouble breathing. In an emergency, call 911.

**A note on what this page covers:** "functional mushrooms" means non-psychedelic mushrooms sold as supplements, powders, teas, and "mushroom coffee." This page is not about psilocybin ("magic") mushrooms, which are a completely different substance with different risks.

## What Are Functional Mushrooms?

Functional mushrooms are edible or medicinal fungi taken for possible health effects rather than as food. Most have a long history in traditional Chinese, Japanese, or Eastern European medicine. Today they're sold as capsules, tinctures, powders stirred into coffee, and pre-mixed "mushroom blends."

The ones you'll see most often:

| Mushroom | Latin name | What people take it for | Strength of human evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lion's mane | *Hericium erinaceus* | Focus, memory, mood, nerve health | Limited: a few small trials |
| Reishi | *Ganoderma lucidum* | Calm, sleep, immune support | Limited and mixed |
| Chaga | *Inonotus obliquus* | Antioxidant, immune support | Very limited: mostly lab and animal work |
| Cordyceps | *Cordyceps militaris* / *Ophiocordyceps sinensis* | Energy, exercise performance | Limited and mixed |
| Turkey tail | *Trametes versicolor* | Immune and gut support | Some clinical use as an add-on cancer therapy in Japan; little for general wellness |

The active ingredients are mostly two kinds of compounds: **beta-glucans** (long sugar chains that interact with the immune system) and **triterpenes** or other small molecules specific to each mushroom. Quality varies widely. Some products are made from the mushroom's fruiting body, others from mycelium grown on grain, which can mean a lot of the powder is actually starch. A product label rarely tells you how much of the active compounds you're getting.

That matters for alcohol, because almost everything we know about these mushrooms comes from lab dishes, mice, and small human studies that didn't involve drinking.

## How Functional Mushrooms Might Interact With Alcohol

There's no single shared mechanism, because each mushroom works differently. But a few themes come up again and again.

### 1. Extra drowsiness (mainly reishi)

Alcohol is a sedative. Reishi has a traditional reputation as a calming, sleep-supporting mushroom, and animal studies suggest it can lengthen sleep. Stacking two things that make you drowsy can leave you more impaired than you realize, especially if you also take a sleep aid. Lion's mane, chaga, cordyceps, and turkey tail are not generally considered sedating.

### 2. Blood sugar

Alcohol can lower blood sugar, especially when you drink without eating or drink heavily, because the liver pauses making new glucose while it's busy processing alcohol. Lab and animal studies suggest several functional mushrooms, including reishi, chaga, cordyceps, and lion's mane, may also lower blood sugar. For most healthy people this is unlikely to matter. For anyone on insulin or diabetes pills, it's a real reason to be careful. Our guide to [alcohol and blood sugar](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025) covers that side in more detail.

### 3. Bleeding

Reishi, and to a lesser extent chaga and lion's mane, have shown anti-clotting effects in lab studies. Alcohol also affects platelets and, when heavy, raises bleeding risk. Together they're unlikely to matter for a healthy person having a couple of drinks. They matter more if you take warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel, or another blood thinner, or if you have surgery scheduled.

### 4. The liver

Here the story is mixed. Many animal studies have tested reishi, chaga, cordyceps, and lion's mane extracts in mice or rats given alcohol, and several reported less liver damage or lower markers of oxidative stress. That sounds encouraging, but animal results often don't carry over to people, and the doses used are usually far higher than what's in a capsule. On the other side, there are a small number of case reports of liver injury in people taking reishi powder. So the honest summary is: **there is no good evidence that functional mushrooms protect your liver from alcohol in humans, and at least one of them carries a rare liver risk of its own.**

### 5. The immune system

Beta-glucans in mushrooms nudge the immune system. Heavy drinking suppresses parts of the immune system. In theory a mushroom might partly offset that, but no human study has shown it. The more practical concern runs the other way: if you take medication to suppress your immune system (after a transplant, or for an autoimmune disease), immune-stimulating mushrooms are something to clear with your doctor whether or not you drink.

## Lion's Mane and Alcohol

Lion's mane is the most popular functional mushroom right now, mostly for focus and memory, so it's the one people ask about most.

**Is it safe to drink on lion's mane?** There's no known dangerous interaction between lion's mane and moderate drinking in healthy adults. Lion's mane isn't sedating, so it doesn't stack with alcohol the way reishi or sleep aids can. It's also eaten as a food in parts of Asia, which suggests normal amounts are well tolerated.

**What the research actually shows.** Lion's mane contains compounds called hericenones and erinacines. In lab and animal studies, these encourage the production of nerve growth factor, a protein that helps nerve cells grow and repair. The most cited human study is a small Japanese trial published in *Phytotherapy Research* in 2009, in which older adults with mild memory decline who took lion's mane for 16 weeks scored better on a cognitive test than those on placebo, with the benefit fading after they stopped. That's interesting, but it was small, it was in older adults, and it had nothing to do with alcohol.

**Does lion's mane undo alcohol's effects on the brain?** There is no good evidence that it does. Alcohol's short-term effects on memory and focus come from how it changes brain signaling while it's in your system, and its long-term harms come from repeated heavy drinking. A supplement that might gently support nerve health over months isn't going to cancel either one. Some animal studies have looked at lion's mane and stomach lining damage caused by alcohol in rats, with protective results, but that hasn't been shown in people.

**Does it help a hangover?** No study has tested it. Marketing that pairs lion's mane with "brain fog" after drinking is borrowing its reputation for focus, not citing hangover research.

**Practical points:** take it at your usual time, keep your drinking moderate, and watch for the side effects that do occur with lion's mane: mild stomach upset, and occasionally skin rashes or allergic reactions, especially in people who are allergic to other mushrooms. If you take diabetes medication or blood thinners, ask your pharmacist first, since lab data hint at small effects on blood sugar and clotting.

## Reishi and Alcohol

Reishi is the mushroom most worth thinking about before a night out, for two reasons: it's the most likely to add to alcohol's sedation, and it's the one with the clearest (though rare) safety signals.

- **Drowsiness.** Reishi is often taken at night for calm and sleep. On nights you drink, take it in the morning or skip it. Don't combine it with alcohol and a sleep aid, sedating antihistamine, or anti-anxiety medication.
- **Bleeding.** Reishi may reduce platelet clumping. If you take a blood thinner or have a bleeding disorder, ask your doctor before using it at all, and stop it about two weeks before surgery unless your doctor tells you otherwise.
- **Blood pressure and blood sugar.** Reishi may lower both slightly. Alcohol can do the same in the hours after drinking. People on medication for either should check with a doctor.
- **Liver.** A handful of published case reports describe liver injury, including at least one fatal case, linked to reishi in powdered form. These are rare, but they're one reason not to think of reishi as a "liver protector" you can lean on while drinking heavily.

Reishi's best-known claims, immune support and better sleep, come from mixed and mostly small studies. Systematic reviews have not found strong evidence for most of its uses. That doesn't mean it does nothing. It means you shouldn't expect it to offset alcohol.

## Chaga and Alcohol

Chaga grows on birch trees and is usually taken as a tea or powder. It's rich in antioxidants in lab tests, and animal studies have looked at it for liver and immune effects.

The specific risk with chaga is **oxalate**. Chaga contains very high levels of oxalate, the same compound behind most kidney stones. Doctors in Japan published a case of serious kidney damage (oxalate nephropathy) in a woman who had taken large amounts of chaga powder daily for months. Heavy drinking adds its own stress on the kidneys through dehydration. For an occasional cup with a moderate drink, this is unlikely to matter. For daily, high-dose chaga in someone who drinks regularly, has kidney disease, or has had kidney stones, it's a real concern. Stay well hydrated, use it in modest amounts, and check with a doctor if you have kidney issues.

Chaga may also lower blood sugar and affect clotting, so the same cautions about diabetes medications and blood thinners apply.

## Cordyceps and Alcohol

Cordyceps is taken for energy and exercise stamina. It isn't a stimulant in the way caffeine is, though some people find it mildly energizing. There's no known direct interaction with alcohol.

The main caution is the same as with other functional mushrooms: it may lower blood sugar and may affect clotting in lab studies, and it may stimulate the immune system. People on diabetes medication, blood thinners, or immune-suppressing drugs should ask their doctor first. As with the others, there is no good evidence that cordyceps reduces hangovers or protects against alcohol damage in people.

## Turkey Tail and Alcohol

Turkey tail is one of the better-studied mushrooms for one narrow use: an extract called PSK has been used for decades in Japan as an add-on to standard cancer treatment. Outside that setting, evidence for everyday immune or gut benefits is thin. There's no known interaction with moderate drinking. If you're taking it alongside cancer treatment, any alcohol decisions should go through your oncology team.

## Mushroom Coffee and Alcohol

Mushroom coffee is usually regular coffee blended with lion's mane, chaga, reishi, or cordyceps. The mushroom content per serving is often small, so the main ingredient that interacts with alcohol is the **caffeine**.

Caffeine doesn't sober you up. It can make you feel more alert while your blood alcohol level stays the same, which can lead people to drink more or make worse decisions about driving. That's the same issue behind mixing alcohol with energy drinks. Our guides to [caffeine and alcohol](/never-hungover/caffeine-and-alcohol) and [coffee for a hangover](/never-hungover/coffee-for-hangover) go into more detail. If your mushroom coffee contains reishi, the mix of caffeine and a mildly sedating mushroom is unusual, but there's no evidence it's harmful in normal amounts.

## Can Functional Mushrooms Help a Hangover?

This is where marketing runs furthest ahead of the evidence. There is no good evidence that lion's mane, reishi, chaga, cordyceps, turkey tail, or any mushroom blend prevents or treats a hangover in people. No published hangover trial that we're aware of has tested them.

The claims usually rest on three things:

1. **Antioxidant activity in lab tests.** Lots of substances look antioxidant in a test tube. That doesn't mean they change how you feel the morning after.
2. **Animal liver studies.** Mice given large doses of mushroom extract and alcohol sometimes show less liver damage. That's a long way from a person taking two capsules before a party.
3. **Reputation for focus or calm.** Lion's mane for "brain fog," reishi for "hangxiety." These borrow general wellness claims and apply them to hangovers without testing them.

What actually reduces hangovers is still mostly behavior: drinking less, drinking slower, eating beforehand, alternating with water, and getting sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers what has the best evidence. If next-day anxiety is your main problem, see our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research).

## Timing: When to Take Functional Mushrooms If You're Drinking

No study has set official timing rules, so these are sensible defaults rather than tested guidelines:

- **Lion's mane, cordyceps, turkey tail:** take them at your usual time. There's no known reason to skip them before a moderate night.
- **Reishi:** take it in the morning on days you plan to drink, and skip any bedtime dose that night.
- **Chaga:** keep it modest and stay hydrated. If you drink heavily, skip high-dose chaga that day.
- **After drinking:** wait until the alcohol has cleared before your next dose of anything sedating. The body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though that varies a lot between people.
- **Mushroom coffee:** fine the next morning, but remember it won't speed up sobering up.

## Who Should Be Careful or Ask a Doctor First

Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining functional mushrooms and alcohol if you:

- Take **blood thinners** such as warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, clopidogrel, or daily aspirin
- Take **insulin or diabetes medication**
- Take **blood pressure medication**
- Take **sedatives, sleep aids, or anti-anxiety medication** (especially relevant for reishi)
- Take **immune-suppressing drugs**, for example after a transplant or for an autoimmune condition
- Have **liver disease, kidney disease, or a history of kidney stones** (especially relevant for chaga)
- Are **pregnant or breastfeeding**, since safety data are lacking
- Have **surgery scheduled**, in which case most doctors advise stopping these supplements about two weeks beforehand
- Are allergic to mushrooms or molds

If you take any prescription medication, our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) explains how to think about supplements, drugs, and alcohol together.

## When to Get Help

Most people who mix a functional mushroom with a few drinks will notice nothing unusual. Get medical advice promptly if you notice:

- Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, or pain under your right ribs (possible liver problem)
- Unusual bruising, nosebleeds, or bleeding gums
- Dizziness, shakiness, sweating, or confusion that could be low blood sugar, especially if you take diabetes medication
- Reduced urine, swelling in your legs, or flank pain after regular chaga use
- A rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing (possible allergic reaction: call 911 for breathing trouble)

And separate from any supplement: if someone who has been drinking can't be woken, is breathing very slowly or irregularly, is vomiting while not fully awake, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, bluish skin, call 911. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a supplement interaction.

## How Functional Mushrooms Compare With Other Supplements People Take Around Drinking

Functional mushrooms usually get lumped in with other "liver" and "recovery" supplements. Here's how they compare on evidence, honestly:

- **Milk thistle** has more human research on the liver than any mushroom, though the results are mixed. See our [milk thistle and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/milk-thistle-and-alcohol).
- **NAC** supplies building blocks for glutathione, the liver's main antioxidant. Evidence for routine use in healthy drinkers is thin. See [NAC and alcohol](/never-hungover/nac-and-alcohol).
- **Ashwagandha** and **kava** are the calming supplements people most often ask about with alcohol, and both carry their own cautions. See [ashwagandha and alcohol](/never-hungover/ashwagandha-and-alcohol) and [kava and alcohol](/never-hungover/kava-and-alcohol).
- **Kudzu** has a few small human studies on drinking behavior itself. See [kudzu and alcohol](/never-hungover/kudzu-and-alcohol).
- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, from the Japanese raisin tree, is the compound this site focuses on. It has been studied specifically for alcohol's effects. Most of that work is in animals, with limited human data, including a 2015 randomized trial in people with fatty liver disease that found improvements in some liver markers. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in everyone.

For a ranked overview with the evidence for each, see our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements).

## If You Want to Try DHM Alongside Mushrooms

No study has tested DHM together with functional mushrooms and alcohol. That said, there's no known reason the two would clash, and some products already combine them. **Toniiq Ease**, for example, pairs DHM with reishi and milk thistle; it's sold as [Toniiq Ease on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07S448GTT?tag=dhmguide-20). If you'd rather keep things simple and avoid reishi's sedation on a night out, a DHM-only product such as [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a lower-cost option, and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) adds L-cysteine and electrolytes. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

None of these, mushroom or DHM, makes heavy drinking safe. They're at best a small add-on to the basics.

## The Bottom Line

- No serious interaction between functional mushrooms and moderate drinking has been reported in healthy adults, but almost no human research has tested the combination.
- **Reishi** is the one to time carefully: it can add to drowsiness and may affect bleeding, blood pressure, and blood sugar, and rare liver injury has been reported.
- **Chaga** is very high in oxalate and has been linked to kidney damage with heavy, long-term use.
- **Lion's mane** isn't sedating and has no known interaction with alcohol, but there's no good evidence it protects your brain from drinking or helps a hangover.
- If you take blood thinners, diabetes or blood pressure medication, sedatives, or immune-suppressing drugs, ask your doctor first.
- There is no good evidence that any functional mushroom prevents or treats hangovers. Drinking less and drinking slower still work best.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is it safe to drink alcohol while taking functional mushrooms?**

For most healthy adults, a normal dose of lion's mane, reishi, chaga, cordyceps, or turkey tail plus a few drinks is not a known dangerous combination. But almost no human studies have tested these mushrooms with alcohol. The main cautions are extra drowsiness with reishi, possible effects on blood sugar and clotting, chaga's high oxalate content, and rare liver injury reported with reishi powder. Keep drinking light, and ask your doctor first if you take blood thinners, diabetes or blood pressure medication, sedatives, or immune-suppressing drugs.

**Can you drink alcohol while taking lion's mane?**

There's no known dangerous interaction between lion's mane and moderate drinking in healthy adults, and lion's mane isn't sedating, so it doesn't stack with alcohol the way some calming supplements do. There are also no human studies of the combination. Take it at your usual time, keep drinking moderate, and ask a pharmacist first if you take diabetes medication or blood thinners, since lab studies hint at small effects on blood sugar and clotting.

**Does lion's mane protect your brain from alcohol?**

There is no good evidence that it does. Lion's mane compounds encourage nerve growth factor in lab and animal studies, and one small Japanese trial found modest memory benefits in older adults with mild cognitive decline. None of that research involved alcohol, and a supplement that might gently support nerve health over months won't cancel alcohol's short-term effects on memory and focus or the harms of regular heavy drinking.

**Can you take reishi and drink alcohol?**

Reishi is the functional mushroom to be most careful with around alcohol. It has a calming reputation and may add to alcohol's drowsiness, and it may slightly lower blood pressure and blood sugar and reduce clotting. Rare cases of liver injury have been reported with reishi powder. On days you drink, take reishi in the morning and skip any bedtime dose, and don't combine it with alcohol and a sleep aid. Ask your doctor first if you take blood thinners or other medication.

**Do functional mushrooms help with hangovers?**

There is no good evidence that any functional mushroom, or mushroom blend, prevents or treats a hangover in people. The claims usually rest on antioxidant results in test tubes, animal liver studies using high doses, or general reputations for focus and calm. What reduces hangovers is still mostly drinking less, drinking slower, eating beforehand, alternating with water, and getting enough sleep.

**Is chaga bad for you if you drink?**

Occasional, modest amounts of chaga are unlikely to be a problem for a healthy person who drinks moderately. The concern is that chaga is very high in oxalate, and a published case from Japan linked months of high-dose chaga powder to serious kidney damage. Heavy drinking can dehydrate you and add stress on the kidneys. If you drink regularly, have kidney disease, or have had kidney stones, avoid daily high-dose chaga and check with a doctor.

**Is mushroom coffee okay with alcohol?**

Mushroom coffee's main active ingredient is usually the caffeine, not the mushrooms. Caffeine doesn't lower your blood alcohol level; it can make you feel more alert while you're just as impaired, which can lead to drinking more or misjudging whether you can drive. A cup the morning after is fine for most people, but it won't sober you up faster.

**Can I take functional mushrooms and DHM together?**

No study has tested functional mushrooms, DHM, and alcohol together, but there's no known reason they would clash, and some products already combine DHM with reishi. If you use reishi, keep in mind its possible drowsiness on a night out. Neither mushrooms nor DHM make heavy drinking safe, and anyone on prescription medication should check with a doctor or pharmacist first.
